questions.title: Stage a single modified file
questions.scenario: You are on `main` in `data-engineering-project`. You edited both `app.py` and `config.py`.
hints: Think about which Git area currently contains each file's changes.
You need a command from the `git add` family.
Stage a path explicitly: `git add <file>`.
questions.explanation: `git add app.py` copies that file's working-tree content into the staging area (index). Other modified files stay unstaged until you add them.
common_mistakes: Using `git add .` which stages every change

questions.title: Commit staged work
questions.objective: Create a commit from the staging area.
questions.task: Create a commit with the message `Add pipeline entrypoint`.
hints: Commits record whatever is currently in the staging area.
Use `git commit` with a message flag.
`git commit -m "your message"`.
questions.explanation: `git commit -m "…"` creates a new snapshot from the index and advances the current branch.
common_mistakes: Trying to commit with nothing staged

questions.title: Inspect repository status
questions.scenario: You just walked into a messy working tree and need situational awareness.
questions.task: Run the command that shows branch, staged, unstaged, and untracked files.
hints: This command does not change the repository.
It is the first command most developers run.
`git status`.
questions.explanation: `git status` is read-only. For this lab, running it successfully while leaving the repo unchanged counts as solving the inspection task.
common_mistakes: Trying to fix files before inspecting

questions.title: Discard changes to one file
questions.scenario:
Repository: `data-engineering-project`
Current branch: `feature/customer-analysis`
Working tree has modifications in `src/customer.py` and `src/orders.py`, plus untracked `notes.txt`.
questions.objective: Use restore to surgically discard working-tree changes.
questions.task: Discard the changes to `src/orders.py` without affecting `src/customer.py` or `notes.txt`.
hints: Think about which Git area currently contains the unwanted edits.
Look at `git restore` for working-tree recovery.
`git restore <path>` restores the path from the index/HEAD.
questions.explanation: `git restore src/orders.py` replaces the working-tree file with the indexed (committed) version. Other files are untouched. Prefer `restore` over older `checkout --` syntax.
common_mistakes: Using `git restore .` and wiping customer.py too

questions.title: Unstage a file
questions.scenario: You accidentally staged `secrets.env` and still want to keep your local edits.
questions.task: Unstage `secrets.env` but keep the file modifications in the working tree.
hints: Think about which Git area currently contains the file.
Look at `git restore` with a staging-area flag.
`git restore --staged <path>`.
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged` removes the path from the index while leaving the working tree alone. That is different from `git restore <path>`, which rewrites the working tree.
common_mistakes: Using `git restore secrets.env` which also discards edits

questions.title: Create a feature branch
questions.scenario: You are on `main` and need an isolated line of work.
questions.objective: Create and switch to a new branch in one step.
hints: You need both a new branch name and to move HEAD there.
`git switch` can create branches with `-c`.
`git switch -c feature/login`.
questions.explanation: `git switch -c feature/login` creates the branch at the current commit and checks it out. Equivalent older form: `git checkout -b feature/login`.
common_mistakes: Creating with `git branch` but forgetting to switch

questions.title: Fast-forward merge a feature
questions.scenario: `feature/metrics` is ahead of `main` with no divergent commits. You are on `main`.
questions.objective: Integrate a feature with a fast-forward merge.
hints: You are already on the branch that should receive the changes.
Use the merge family of commands.
`git merge feature/metrics`.
questions.explanation: Because `main` was a direct ancestor of `feature/metrics`, Git can fast-forward `main` to that tip without creating a merge commit.
common_mistakes: Merging while on the feature branch
Rebasing when a FF merge is enough

questions.title: Stash local work
questions.scenario: You have uncommitted edits but need a clean tree to switch context.
questions.task: Stash your local modifications so the working tree becomes clean.
hints: You need a temporary shelf for unfinished work.
Look at the stash command family.
`git stash` (or `git stash push`).
questions.explanation: `git stash` records local modifications and resets the working tree/index to HEAD. Use `stash pop`/`apply` later to restore.

questions.title: Fix an accidental stage
questions.scenario: You meant to stage `src/api.py` but staged `src/legacy.py` instead.
questions.task: Unstage `src/legacy.py` while keeping its working-tree edits. (Next, you would stage `src/api.py` — practice that as a follow-up once this is clean.)
hints: You need to move changes out of the staging area — not discard them.
Look at `git restore` with a staging-area flag.
`git restore --staged src/legacy.py`.
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged src/legacy.py` removes the path from the index while leaving the working tree alone. Afterwards you can `git add src/api.py` when you are ready.
common_mistakes: Using `git restore src/legacy.py` which also discards edits

questions.title: Add an origin remote
questions.scenario: Your local repo has commits but no remotes configured yet.
questions.task: Add a remote named `origin` with URL `https://github.com/example/practice.git`.
hints: Remotes are named bookmarks for other repositories.
Use the `git remote` family.
`git remote add origin <url>`.
questions.explanation: `git remote add` only records a URL locally. It does not fetch or push until you run those commands.
common_mistakes: Using clone when a repo already exists

questions.title: Undo the last local commit (keep changes)
questions.scenario: You committed too early on `main`. The commit has not been pushed. You want the changes back in the staging area.
questions.objective: Move HEAD back one commit without losing the snapshot contents.
questions.task: Reset the last commit but keep its changes staged.
hints: You want to move a branch pointer without discarding file contents.
Look at `git reset` modes — soft vs mixed vs hard.
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`.
questions.explanation: `--soft` moves HEAD/branch back but leaves the index and working tree as they were, so the undone commit's changes remain staged.

questions.title: Delete a merged feature branch
questions.scenario: Feature work is merged. Clean up the local branch name while staying on `main`.
hints: Branch names are pointers — deleting one does not delete commits that are still reachable from main.
Use `git branch` with a delete flag.
`git branch -d feature/done`.
questions.explanation: `git branch -d` removes the local branch ref. Commits remain reachable from `main` after the merge/fast-forward.
common_mistakes: Trying to delete the branch you are on
